prompt.context: Two companies are the only competitors in an industry and produce exactly the same product. Your client was the pioneer in the industry and has controlled 70% of the market for many years. Their competitor has always followed price changes initiated by your client. Recently though, the competitor has aggressively lowered prices 15% and has cut into your client's market share reducing it to 60%. Your client's profit margins are only 14%, so they are hesitant to match the price cut, but they are afraid that they will continue to lose share if they don't. Assume that there is no threat of new competitors entering the market and that there are no substitute products. All inputs are commodities and are readily available. The end-users are sophisticated and make their purchasing decisions based mostly on price.
prompt.question: How has the competitor managed to cut prices so dramatically and still make money, and what would you advise your client to do?

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to industry growth?
clarifying_info.a: Industry growth has historically been 5% per year but has flattened out completely in the last year.

clarifying_info.q: What do we know about the buyers?
clarifying_info.a: There are many buyers and the price of this product is a negligible input cost for them.

clarifying_info.q: What is the financial situation of each company?
clarifying_info.a: Your client and its competitor are both financially strong divisions of larger unrelated companies.

clarifying_info.q: What does the cost structure look like?
clarifying_info.a: Raw materials make up 50% of the total cost of producing this product. All other costs are fixed.

clarifying_info.q: Are the production processes similar between the two competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Both competitors use essentially the same process and have very similar cost structures.
Capacity can only be modified in large increments and the competitor brought on a new line 6 months ago.

framework: Recognize this is a capacity utilization problem, not a standard Porter's Five Forces problem — the product cannot be differentiated
Understand the competitor's cost economics: new capacity line → overcapacity → incentive to cut price to drive volume
Quantify the impact on unit costs for both sides as volume shifts
Apply game theory to determine the optimal strategic response for the client
Formulate a recommendation covering price matching, regaining share, and long-run pricing leadership

questions.prompt: How did the competitor manage to cut prices 15% and still remain profitable?
questions.guidance: The competitor added a new capacity line 6 months ago, creating overcapacity. With 50% of costs fixed, spreading those fixed costs over greater volume reduces average unit cost. Market share rose from 30% to 40%, a 33% volume increase. At 50% variable cost, unit costs fell by approximately 16.5%, more than offsetting the 15% price cut.

math.setup: Market is constant in size. Competitor market share: 30% → 40%. Volume increase = (40-30)/30 = 33%. Fixed cost share = 50%. Reduction in average unit cost = volume increase × fixed cost share.
steps: Net effect: unit cost fell 16.5% while price fell 15%, so competitor is better off, and volume is up 33%
math.answer: The competitor's average unit cost fell ~16.5%, which more than offset the 15% price cut; combined with 33% volume growth, their profit improved significantly.

questions.prompt: What is the impact on your client's unit costs from the market share loss?
questions.guidance: Client market share dropped from 70% to 60%. With constant market size, volume fell by (70-60)/70 ≈ 14%. With 50% fixed costs, average unit cost rose by approximately 7%.

math.setup: Client market share: 70% → 60%. Volume decrease = (70-60)/70 ≈ 14%. Fixed cost share = 50%. Increase in average unit cost = volume decrease × fixed cost share.
steps: Not matching the price cut means continued share loss and rising unit costs
math.answer: Client's average unit cost rose ~7% due to volume loss, eroding the already thin 14% margin further.

questions.prompt: Using game theory, what should the client do?
questions.guidance: The client should match the competitor's price cut immediately to signal that undercutting will not go unpunished. Being larger (60% vs 40% share), the client has a slight cost advantage and can sustain a price war better. After demonstrating willingness to compete on price, the client should aggressively offer inducements to win back recently lost customers. Once the competitor recognizes it cannot win a price war, the client should incrementally raise prices and ensure the competitor follows — re-establishing the historical price-follower dynamic. Because the product cost is a negligible input for buyers, gradual price increases are unlikely to trigger buyer resistance.

brainstorming.prompt: What actions can the client take to regain lost market share and re-establish pricing leadership?

categories.name: Defensive pricing
ideas: Match the competitor's 15% price cut immediately
Signal credibly that any further undercut will be matched

categories.name: Regaining customers
ideas: Offer short-term inducements (volume discounts, extended payment terms) to recently defected customers
Leverage long-standing relationships from pioneer status

categories.name: Cost management
ideas: Seek ways to reduce variable costs to widen margin at lower prices
Explore whether own capacity can be more efficiently utilized

categories.name: Re-establishing price leadership
ideas: Incrementally raise prices once the competitor accepts price parity
Monitor competitor's follow-through on price increases to confirm follower behavior is restored

categories.name: Longer-term strategy
ideas: Assess whether market growth will resume, which would ease capacity pressure on both sides
Evaluate potential for modest product or service differentiation to reduce pure price competition

recommendation: Match the competitor's 15% price cut immediately to halt further market share erosion and signal that price undercutting will be met
Aggressively offer inducements to recently lost customers to regain share, leveraging the client's larger scale and cost advantage
Once parity is restored and the competitor recognizes it cannot win a price war, incrementally raise prices and re-establish the historical price-leader/follower dynamic
risks: A prolonged price war could compress both companies' margins before the competitor blinks
If the competitor's parent company subsidizes losses, the price war could last longer than expected
Buyer concentration is low and product cost is negligible for buyers, so regaining customers may require sustained inducements
next_steps: Confirm cost structure details to precisely quantify margin impact at different price/volume scenarios
Implement targeted outreach to the 10 percentage points of lost market share with tailored offers
Monitor competitor pricing weekly and match any further cuts within days to maintain credible deterrence
